processing: As with other ripe pu-erh, sun-dried maocha goes through wet piling (wo dui) and drying; the tea is then steamed and pressed into a flat square brick.
harvest_season: No fixed season belongs to the name; ripe pu-erh is usually blended from leaf of different pickings, and the pressing year is what gets printed on the wrapper.
appearance_dry: A flat, tightly pressed square of dark reddish-brown leaf, often small enough to sit in one hand.
appearance_liquor: Deep red-brown to near black, as is typical of ripe pu-erh.
appearance_wet: Broken and whole dark brown leaf, soft after steeping.
taste_profile: As with ripe pu-erh in general, expect earthy, woody depth and a smooth, low-bitterness body; the character depends on the blend, not the square shape.

brewing.notes: Pry off a piece along the edge and rinse once or twice. Near-boiling water suits ripe pu-erh; a tightly pressed brick needs a steep or two to open.

vintage_note: Sold by pressing year and by weight, with 100 g squares among the formats on the market. As is usual for ripe pu-erh, most is drunk within about ten years, and a few years of rest takes the edge off a fresh pile taste. The wrapper year says when it was pressed, which may not be when the leaf was picked.
description:
Fang zhuan simply means square brick. It names a shape, not a place or a recipe, so two square bricks can have little in common beyond their outline. The ripe version is a handy small format of shu pu-erh.

Bricks and cakes are made from broadly the same material and differ mainly in the mould. The leaf is ripened in a wet pile, as with any shu, then steamed and pressed. Tight pressing is what you notice most in practice: it slows the first steep and makes the tea a little fiddly to break.

In the cup, treat it like other ripe pu-erh: earth, wood and a smooth sweetness, little bitterness. Rinse it, use very hot water and keep early steeps short. If the first cup is thin, the pressed core has not opened yet, so give it another steep before judging it.

When buying, look for the maker, the pressing year and the weight, because the word on the label promises nothing about quality. A strong fishy or sour pile smell in a young brick is a reason to let it air out or to choose another one.
history: Little is documented about fang zhuan as a distinct tea. Bricks are one of the long-standing compressed forms of pu-erh, and the square is one variation on that form, made by various producers rather than tied to a known inventor or date.
